name: SpaceX
one_liner: Builds reusable rockets and spacecraft to slash the cost of reaching orbit, with the long-term aim of making life multiplanetary.
story: Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 to cut launch costs and eventually reach Mars, a plan most of the aerospace establishment considered unrealistic; its first three Falcon 1 launches failed (the third in August 2008) and the company survived on a $20M Founders Fund round and a NASA cargo contract. It went on to land and re-fly orbital boosters, bought xAI in February 2026 in a deal valuing SpaceX at about $1T, and listed on Nasdaq (SPCX) on June 12, 2026, raising about $75B at $135/share (about $1.77T valuation) in the largest IPO in history. peak_valuation_usd is the roughly $2.1T market cap reported at the first-day close (later peaks not checked); the 2015 Google/Fidelity round was reported at a $10-12B valuation.

near_death.what: Third consecutive Falcon 1 failure in August 2008 (stage separation timing error) put NASA contract prospects and the company's cash in doubt; a $20M Founders Fund investment arrived the same month and the fourth flight reached orbit in September 2008.
NASA Commercial Resupply Services contract (about $1.6B for 12 cargo flights) awarded in December 2008 kept the company alive.

dismissed_by.who: Neil Armstrong and Gene Cernan (Apollo astronauts)
dismissed_by.quote_or_fact: Paraphrase: In 2010-2011 congressional testimony both questioned the shift of human spaceflight to commercial newcomers, citing many unsolved technical challenges; Musk called them his heroes and said he wished they would visit SpaceX.
Paraphrase: Analysts said the third straight failure could jeopardize SpaceX's ability to compete for valuable NASA space station contracts.

name: Starlink
one_liner: SpaceX's low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation selling broadband internet directly to consumers, businesses and governments worldwide.
story: Starlink is a business line inside SpaceX (not a separate company), announced in 2015 and funded from SpaceX's own balance sheet, so it has no separate rounds or valuation. It sounded doomed because every earlier LEO broadband constellation (Iridium, Globalstar, Orbcomm, Teledesic) went bankrupt, and Musk himself framed the goal as simply avoiding bankruptcy; cheap launches on SpaceX's own reusable Falcon 9 changed the math. It grew to about $11.4B revenue in 2025 and 13.6M consumer subscribers by September 30, 2026, and was the main engine behind SpaceX's June 2026 IPO (no separate Starlink listing).

dismissed_by.quote_or_fact: Headline: "Elon Musk's Starlink risks being another satellite flop"

dismissed_by.who: History of LEO constellations, as cited by Musk (Satellite 2020)
dismissed_by.quote_or_fact: Paraphrase: Musk noted that essentially every prior low-Earth-orbit constellation had gone bankrupt and said Starlink's goal was to be the first not to.

name: Tesla
one_liner: Electric car maker that started with a high-priced sports car to fund a path to mass-market EVs, batteries and energy storage.
story: Tesla bet that a startup could build electric cars from scratch when no new US automaker had succeeded in decades and EVs were seen as slow, short-range niche products; it began with the expensive Roadster to fund cheaper models. Musk supplied about $6.5M of the 2004 $7.5M Series A, Daimler bought a roughly 10% stake for about $50M in May 2009, a $465M DOE loan was approved in June 2009 (repaid in May 2013, years early), and Tesla listed on June 29, 2010 at $17/share, raising $226M. Market cap at listing and peak market cap were not verified in this session, so those fields are null.

near_death.what: During the 2008 financial crisis Tesla nearly ran out of cash while the Roadster ramped; Musk put in more of his own money and a round closed in December 2008, before the 2009 Daimler investment and DOE loan.
Model 3 'production hell' in 2017-2018; Musk later said the company came close to bankruptcy during the ramp.
